claims.evidence: This describes the data collection methodology supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Observers walked along each transect at a constant speed (2.0 km/hr) and recorded all the birds seen or heard on the survey islands.
claims.source: In each survey, observers walked along each transect at a constant speed (2.0 km/hr) and recorded all the birds seen or heard on the survey islands.
claims.evidence: This describes the data collection methodology.

claims.claim: The abundance estimate was based on the maximum number of individuals recorded across the nine annual surveys.
claims.source: We based our abundance estimate on the maximum number of individuals recorded across the nine annual surveys.
claims.evidence: This describes the data processing methodology.

claims.claim: Non-breeding species, nocturnal and crepuscular species, high-flying species passing over the islands, and strongly water-associated birds were excluded from the record.
claims.source: We excluded non-breeding species, nocturnal and crepuscular species, high-flying species passing over the islands (e.g., raptors, swallows) and strongly water-associated birds (e.g., cormorants) from our record.
claims.evidence: This describes the data filtering criteria.

claims.claim: 60 species were finally retained after filtering.
claims.source: Following these filtering, 60 species were finally retained.
claims.evidence: This describes the final dataset after filtering.

claims.claim: Climate data (monthly average temperature from 2012 to 2021) was obtained from the Meteorological Bureau of Chun'an County in Zhejiang Province, China.
claims.source: We obtained climate data (monthly average temperature from 2012 to 2021) from the Meteorological Bureau of Chun'an County in Zhejiang Province, China.
claims.evidence: This describes the source of climate data.

claims.claim: Breeding season temperature was calculated as the average of the mean monthly temperature from April to June.
claims.source: We calculated breeding season temperature as the average of the mean monthly temperature from April to June in order to represent the thermal conditions birds experience at this site each year (Lindström et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This describes the data processing methodology supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Breeding season temperature increased significantly over 10 years (slope = 0.078, r2=34.53%, p=0.04).
claims.source: Breeding season temperature increased significantly over 10 years (slope = 0.078, r2=34.53%, p=0.04, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of climate data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: STI of a given species is defined as the average temperature of breeding months (April – June) across its distributional range (restricted to the Northern hemisphere) averaged over 1970–2000.
claims.source: We followed the methods of Devictor et al., 2008 to calculate a species temperature index (STI) using ArcMap 10.3. STI of a given species is defined as the average temperature of breeding months (April – June) across its distributional range (restricted to the Northern hemisphere) averaged over 1970–2000.
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology for calculating STI supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Monthly temperature data were obtained from WorldClim at a resolution of 30-arc seconds.
claims.source: Monthly temperature data were obtained from WorldClim at a resolution of 30-arc seconds (http://www.worldclim.org).
claims.evidence: This describes the source of temperature data for STI calculation.

claims.claim: Distributional maps were extracted from Birdlife International 2019.
claims.source: Distributional maps were extracted from Birdlife International 2019 (http://datazone.birdlife.org/species/requestdis), in which we selected only the distributional regions where the species is either resident or breeding.
claims.evidence: This describes the source of distributional data for STI calculation.

claims.claim: Species with STI higher than the median STI were labeled as warm-adapted species, and species lower than the median STI were labeled as cold-adapted species.
claims.source: All species were divided into two groups indicating their relative thermal preference: species with STI higher than the median STI were labeled as warm-adapted species, and species lower than the median STI were labeled as cold-adapted species (Bates et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes the classification methodology supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The rank order of species STI is highly correlated across methods.
claims.source: The STI of a species can differ depending on distributional and climate data but the rank order of species STI is highly correlated across methods (Barnagaud et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The robustness of STI calculations was verified using different distributional ranges and annual time windows.
claims.source: We verified the robustness of our STI calculations using different distributional ranges and annual time windows (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This describes a validation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: CTI is a community-level index representing the average species thermal niche of all species or individuals in the community.
claims.source: CTI is a community-level index representing the average species thermal niche of all species or individuals in the community (Devictor et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation.

claims.claim: True abundance should be highly correlated with maximum observed abundance given high survey effort.
claims.source: CTIoccur was calculated using occurrence data corrected for imperfect detection (see next section), while CTIabun was estimated using the maximum annual count across 9 surveys. Given that our survey effort was so high (i.e., 9 repeat surveys per year), true abundance should be highly correlated with maximum observed abundance (MacKenzie et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological justification supported by a citation.

claims.claim: A spatially hierarchical dynamic multi-species occupancy model was developed in a Bayesian framework to account for imperfect detection.
claims.source: Presence-absence data can be highly sensitive to false negatives, so to explore the driving processes of change in CTIoccur, and to explore how habitat fragmentation mediated the main processes while accounting for the imperfect detection, we developed a spatially hierarchical dynamic multi-species occupancy model (MSOM) in a Bayesian framework based on the model by Royle and Kéry, 2007.
claims.evidence: This describes the statistical methodology supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Occupancy estimates are broadly interpreted as 'use' to relax the closure assumption.
claims.source: However, given that individual birds move dynamically across territories within a year, during 9 surveys each year, we broadly interpret our estimates of 'occupancy' as 'use' (Si et al., 2018) to relax the closure assumption (MacKenzie et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological clarification supported by citations.

claims.claim: The Bayesian p-value was 0.488, indicating an unbiased estimation of the model.
claims.source: We checked the posterior predictive ability of the model fit by calculating Bayesian p-values (p=0.488, indicating an unbiased estimation of our model; Gelman et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is a result from model validation supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Bayesian linear regression was used to derive a posterior estimate of the temporal trend in CTIoccur while propagating error in the estimation of CTIoccur.
claims.source: To test for occurrence-based thermophilization at the island level, Bayesian linear regression using R2jags (Su and Yajima, 2021) was used to derive a posterior estimate of the temporal trend in CTIoccur while propagating error in the estimation of CTIoccur.
claims.evidence: This describes the statistical methodology supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Linear mixed effect models with restricted maximum likelihood were used to model temporal trends in CTIabun.
claims.source: To test for abundance-based thermophilization, linear mixed effect models (LMM) with restricted maximum likelihood (REML) were used to model temporal trends in CTIabun using function lme in R package nlme (Pinheiro et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes the statistical methodology supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The first-order correlation structure was included to account for temporal autocorrelation of CTI from the same island through time.
claims.source: To account for the temporal autocorrelation of CTI from the same island through time, we included the first-order correlation structure (e.g. the corAR1 structure) because observations sampled from the nearby years may be more similar.
claims.evidence: This describes the statistical methodology to account for temporal autocorrelation.

results.result: The study collected 10 years of bird community data (2012-2021) from 36 islands in the Thousand Island Lake system, a subtropical reservoir formed in 1959. The study period experienced significant climatic warming (slope = 0.078, p=0.04), with breeding season temperature increasing over the decade. The sampling design included 53 transects surveyed nine times annually during breeding season (April-June), with 60 species retained after filtering.
results.evaluation: The methodological claims are well-documented with specific details about study design, sampling effort, temporal coverage, and climate trends. The significant warming trend (C121) is statistically supported with appropriate metrics. The study system description and data collection protocols are clearly specified and internally consistent.

results.result: Species Temperature Index (STI) was calculated for 60 bird species using established methods, with values averaging 19.94±3.58°C and ranging from 9.30°C to 27.20°C. STI showed no significant correlation with ecological traits (dispersal ability, body size, body mass, clutch size, diet, active layer, residence type). Species were classified as warm-adapted (STI > median) or cold-adapted (STI < median), with the robustness of STI calculations verified across different distributional ranges and time windows.
results.evaluation: The STI methodology is well-established (citing Devictor et al., 2008) and appropriately applied. The lack of correlation between STI and ecological traits (C47-C49) is properly tested statistically. Robustness checks (C127) strengthen confidence in the STI metric. The classification approach using median split is standard and appropriate for the analysis.

results.result: Thermophilization was detected at both landscape and transect scales, but with different patterns. At the landscape scale, only abundance-based CTI showed a significant increasing trend (slope=0.327±0.041, p<0.001), while occurrence-based CTI showed no trend. At the individual transect level, both occurrence-based (mean trend=0.124, 95% CrI: 0.108-0.137) and abundance-based CTI (slope=0.320±0.021, p<0.001) showed significant increases, with the abundance response considerably stronger than occurrence.
results.evaluation: The differential responses between CTI metrics and spatial scales are clearly documented with appropriate statistical support. The finding that abundance-based CTI responds more strongly than occurrence-based CTI is consistent with cited literature (C79) and suggests population-level changes precede distributional changes. The Bayesian credible intervals and p-values support the conclusions.

results.result: Thermophilization was driven by differential colonization-extinction dynamics between warm- and cold-adapted species. Warm-adapted species showed increasing colonization rates (slope=0.259, p=0.043), decreasing extinction rates, and increasing occupancy and abundance over time. Cold-adapted species showed the opposite pattern with decreasing colonization, increasing extinction (slope=-0.414, p=0.015), and declining occupancy and abundance. These opposing trends resulted in a strong negative correlation (r=-0.77) between colonization and extinction trends across species.
results.evaluation: The mechanistic decomposition of thermophilization into colonization-extinction dynamics is well-supported by statistical analyses with appropriate p-values and effect sizes. The strong correlation (C59) between colonization and extinction trends provides compelling evidence for thermal affinity as a driver. The consistency across multiple metrics (occupancy, abundance, richness) strengthens the conclusions. Figure 4 provides clear visual support.

results.result: Island isolation consistently mediated thermophilization dynamics: on less isolated islands (nearer to mainland), all 15 warm-adapted species increased colonization rates faster over time, while 21 of 23 cold-adapted species increased extinction rates faster. This pattern supports dispersal limitation as a primary mechanism by which habitat fragmentation mediates species range shifts under climate warming.
results.evaluation: The isolation effects are remarkably consistent across species (15/15 warm-adapted, 21/23 cold-adapted showing expected patterns), providing strong evidence for dispersal limitation. The interpretation (C95) is well-supported by the data and consistent with cited literature. The multi-species occupancy model appropriately accounts for imperfect detection and spatial structure. Figure 5 clearly illustrates these patterns.

results.result: Island area had mixed effects on colonization-extinction dynamics. For most warm-adapted species (11 of 15), colonization rates increased faster on smaller islands, while cold-adapted species showed approximately equal splits between faster extinction on smaller (12/23) versus larger islands (11/23). Temperature monitoring data confirmed that smaller islands had diminished temperature buffering ability, supporting microclimate as a primary driver of fragmentation's mediation of thermophilization.
results.evaluation: The area effects are more complex than isolation effects, but the empirical temperature data (C96) provides direct mechanistic support for the microclimate buffering hypothesis. The mixed patterns for cold-adapted species suggest multiple mechanisms may be operating. The post-hoc temperature monitoring (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) strengthens the mechanistic interpretation, though it was collected in only one year (2022) on 20 islands.

results.result: The study found evidence of thermophilization driven by increasing warm-adapted species and decreasing cold-adapted species in terms of colonization rate, extinction rate, occupancy rate, and population size. Critically, colonization rates of warm-adapted species increased faster on smaller or less isolated islands, while cold-adapted species were lost more quickly on closer islands. This provides support for dispersal limitation and microclimate buffering as primary mechanisms by which habitat fragmentation mediates species range shift.
results.evaluation: These are the primary findings of the study, well-supported by the detailed analyses in other result groups. The claims integrate multiple lines of evidence (CTI trends, species-specific dynamics, fragmentation effects) into a coherent conclusion. The mechanistic interpretation (C8) is appropriately cautious, identifying dispersal limitation and microclimate buffering as 'primary proxies' rather than definitive mechanisms.

results.result: The landscape-scale analysis revealed that thermophilization was mostly due to occurrence dynamics within the region rather than exogenous community turnover. STI was identified as an effective broad indicator of relative climatic vulnerability, with species having higher thermal preferences generally benefiting from local climate warming.
results.evaluation: The inference about within-region dynamics (C80) is logically derived from the difference between landscape and transect-level results. The conclusion about STI as a vulnerability indicator (C82-C83) is well-supported by the strong relationships between STI and temporal trends in colonization, extinction, and abundance, and is consistent with cited literature (C84).

results.result: Despite general trends, not all warm-adapted species increased and not all cold-adapted species decreased, indicating that species did not contribute equally to thermophilization.
results.evaluation: This nuanced observation is evident in Figures 4 and 5, which show variation in species responses. The acknowledgment of heterogeneity strengthens rather than weakens the overall conclusions by demonstrating appropriate scientific caution. This is consistent with cited literature (C94) showing similar patterns elsewhere.

results.result: A spatially hierarchical dynamic multi-species occupancy model (MSOM) was developed in a Bayesian framework to account for imperfect detection, with occupancy interpreted as 'use' to relax closure assumptions. Model validation showed good fit (Bayesian p-value=0.488). Bayesian linear regression and linear mixed effects models with temporal autocorrelation structures were used to analyze CTI trends.
results.evaluation: The statistical methodology is appropriate and well-justified. The MSOM approach properly accounts for imperfect detection, a critical issue in occupancy studies. The Bayesian p-value (C132) indicates unbiased model estimation. The interpretation of occupancy as 'use' (C131) is a reasonable accommodation for mobile species surveyed multiple times per year. The temporal autocorrelation structure (C135) appropriately addresses non-independence of repeated measures.

results.result: The study provides conservation recommendations: better connected landscapes should be developed to remove dispersal constraints; small patches can foster establishment of warm-adapted species while large patches can act as refugia for cold-adapted species; preserving patches of diverse sizes can provide stepping stones or shelters depending on species' thermal affinity.
results.evaluation: These conservation recommendations logically follow from the empirical findings about isolation and area effects. However, they are inferences about management implications rather than direct empirical results. The recommendations are appropriately cautious and acknowledge the differential roles of patch size for species with different thermal affinities.

results.result: The study proposed three theoretical mechanisms by which habitat fragmentation could mediate thermophilization: (1) reduced microclimate buffering in small patches boosting warm-adapted species colonization and cold-adapted species extinction; (2) reduced habitat heterogeneity in fragmented patches intensifying loss of cold-adapted species and weakening colonization of warm-adapted species; (3) dispersal limitation from isolation preventing colonization of warm-adapted species and emigration of cold-adapted species.
results.evaluation: These are a priori hypotheses (illustrated in Figure 1) rather than empirical results. While the study found support for mechanisms 1 and 3 (microclimate buffering and dispersal limitation), the evidence for mechanism 2 (habitat heterogeneity) is less direct. The claims are appropriately framed as expectations ('may boost', 'should experience') but their status as hypotheses rather than findings should be clear.

results.result: The study site (TIL) is positioned near the cold edge of most warm-adapted species' ranges. Combined with predictions that birds in China should move upslope or poleward under climate change, the authors infer that local climate will continue to shift warm-adapted species toward thermal optima, predicting continued population growth.
results.evaluation: This is a speculative prediction about future trends (C90) based on biogeographic positioning (C88) and cited predictions (C89). While the logic is sound, it extends beyond the 10-year study period and assumes continued warming and stable species distributions elsewhere. The prediction is appropriately framed as an inference but lacks empirical validation.

results.result: The authors speculate that some cold-adapted species showing increased extinction on larger islands may face stronger predation pressures, as predators like snakes and felids may increase activity under climate warming and only exist on larger islands in this system.
results.evaluation: This is explicitly acknowledged as post-hoc speculation (C100) to explain unexpected patterns for species like Spizixos semitorques and Pericrocotus cantonensis (C70). While the cited evidence about predator activity under warming exists, there is no direct data on predation rates or predator distributions in this study. This represents an interesting hypothesis for future work but is not empirically supported here.

results.result: The study demonstrates thermophilization in the bird community over 10 years, driven by increasing warm-adapted species and decreasing cold-adapted species. This was evident in both occurrence- and abundance-based CTI metrics, with abundance showing a stronger response. The process was driven by increased colonization and decreased extinction of warm-adapted species, and the opposite pattern for cold-adapted species.
results.evaluation: Both reviewers explicitly affirm these findings. The editor states the authors 'provide convincing evidence using appropriate and validated methodologies' and the anonymous reviewer confirms 'they found that indeed there was thermophilization happening during the last 10 years, which was more pronounced for the CTI based on abundances.' The reviewer describes the conclusions as 'sound, and mostly well supported by the results.'

results.result: Colonization rates of warm-adapted species increased faster temporally on less isolated islands. Specifically, on islands nearer to the mainland, 15 out of 15 investigated warm-adapted species increased their colonization probability at a higher rate over time.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly summarizes this finding: 'they show that also both thermophilization processes (increase of warm and decrease of cold-adapted species) was stronger on islands closer to the mainland, due to closer sources to species populations.' The editor affirms the study provides 'convincing evidence' about 'how island area and isolation affect the colonization of warm-adapted species.'

results.result: Cold-adapted species were lost more quickly temporally on closer (less isolated) islands. Most cold-adapted species (21 out of 23 species) increased their extinction probability at a higher rate on islands nearer to the mainland.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer confirms this finding, stating that 'both thermophilization processes (increase of warm and decrease of cold-adapted species) was stronger on islands closer to the mainland' and attributes this to 'limited dispersal (i.e. range shift potential) in more isolated islands.' The editor also affirms the evidence regarding 'extinction of cold-adapted species.'

results.result: For most warm-adapted species (11 out of 15 investigated species), colonization rates increased faster over time on smaller islands. This pattern was consistent with the hypothesis that smaller islands have lower climate buffering.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly describes this finding: 'they unravel some of the mechanisms behind this dynamic by showing that warm-adapted species increased while cold-dwelling decreased more strongly on smaller islands, which is - according to the authors - due to lowered thermal buffering on smaller islands (which was supported by air temperature monitoring done during the study period on small and large islands).'

results.result: Temperature buffering ability was diminished on smaller islands, supporting microclimate as a primary driver of fragmentation's mediation of thermophilization. This was demonstrated using understory air temperature data monitored on 20 islands.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly acknowledges this supporting evidence, noting it was 'supported by air temperature monitoring done during the study period on small and large islands.' The reviewer treats this as important mechanistic support for the main findings about island area effects.

results.result: The study provides support for dispersal limitation and microclimate buffering as primary proxies by which habitat fragmentation mediates species range shift. Isolation from population sources can limit the dispersal that underlies range shifts.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer affirms the interpretation of mechanisms, stating the authors 'present interesting mechanisms without being too bold on their findings.' The editor describes the study as providing 'insight into how ecosystems and communities respond to climate change' and the reviewer notes the findings support understanding of 'dispersal limitation' effects.

results.result: For cold-adapted species, extinction rates showed mixed patterns with island area: approximately equally split between increasing faster on smaller islands (12 out of 23 species) and larger islands (11 out of 23 species). Two species showed significantly increasing rates of extinction on larger islands.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer acknowledges this mixed finding, noting 'Island area, in contrast, had a more mixed role in moderating colonization/extinction rates across species' and describes the variation in responses. The reviewer treats this complexity as appropriately handled by the authors.

results.result: Distance to the mainland is the best distance-based measure for fitting species' colonization and extinction rates in the Thousand Island Lake system, as established by previous research in this system.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer raises a methodological concern about this choice: 'The metric of island isolation based on distance to the mainland seems a bit too oversimplified as in real-life the study system rather represents an island network where the islands of different sizes are in varying distances to each other.' However, the reviewer acknowledges 'the authors do explain the reason for this metric, backed up by earlier research' and notes 'the fact, that the authors did find a signal of island isolation does support their method.'

results.result: The study period experienced consistent climatic warming, with breeding season temperature increasing significantly over 10 years (slope = 0.078, r²=34.53%, p=0.04).
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer confirms this aspect of the study design, noting the authors 'used extensive bird monitoring data... covering 10 years' during a period of warming. Neither reviewer questions the climate data or warming trend. The editor affirms the study examines effects 'during a period of consistent climatic warming.'

results.result: The study used extensive bird monitoring data collected over 10 years across 36 islands with 53 survey transects, with nine surveys per year per island (three times per month from April to June, 2012-2021).
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly praises the methodology: 'They used extensive bird monitoring data (9 surveys per year per island) across 36 islands of varying size and isolation from the mainland covering 10 years.' The editor describes the methodologies as 'appropriate and validated.' The reviewer states 'The study questions and hypotheses are very well aligned with the methods used, ranging from field surveys to extensive modeling frameworks.'

results.result: A spatially hierarchical dynamic multi-species occupancy model was developed in a Bayesian framework to account for imperfect detection, with model validation showing unbiased estimation (Bayesian p-value = 0.488).
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer affirms the modeling approach, stating 'The authors use extensive modeling frameworks' and describing the methods as 'well balanced.' The editor confirms the authors used 'appropriate and validated methodologies.' Neither reviewer raises concerns about the occupancy modeling approach or its validation.

comparisons.comparison: Strong agreement on thermophilization findings. Both affirm the colonization-extinction dynamics driven by thermal affinity (C55-C63). OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation while peer reviewers confirm the evidence is 'convincing' and conclusions are 'sound and well supported.' Both evaluate these core findings as SUPPORTED.

Both support differential CTI responses (C50-C52, C77-C78). OpenEval emphasizes the methodological distinction between abundance-based and occurrence-based CTI, while peer reviewers confirm thermophilization was 'more pronounced for the CTI based on abundances.' Both find this SUPPORTED.

Both affirm the primary study findings (C5-C8, C71). OpenEval notes these integrate multiple lines of evidence into coherent conclusions, while peer reviewers describe the evidence as 'convincing' using 'appropriate and validated methodologies.' Both evaluate as SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on isolation effects for dispersal limitation (C64-C66, C72-C73). OpenEval highlights the remarkable consistency across species (15/15 warm-adapted, 21/23 cold-adapted), while peer reviewers confirm findings were 'stronger on islands closer to the mainland, due to closer sources to species populations.' Both SUPPORTED.

Both support isolation effects on cold-adapted species extinction (C66, C73). OpenEval emphasizes the multi-species occupancy model accounting for imperfect detection, while peer reviewers attribute patterns to 'limited dispersal (i.e. range shift potential) in more isolated islands.' Both SUPPORTED.

Both address colonization of warm-adapted species (C6). OpenEval integrates this into primary findings with appropriate caution about mechanisms, while peer reviewers specifically confirm the increase of warm-adapted species on less isolated islands. Both SUPPORTED.

Both support extinction patterns of cold-adapted species (C7). OpenEval frames this as part of the integrated primary findings, while peer reviewers explicitly confirm 'decrease of cold-adapted species' was stronger on less isolated islands. Both SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on island area effects and microclimate buffering (C67-C70). OpenEval notes the complexity and empirical temperature support (C96), while peer reviewers confirm warm-adapted species increased more on smaller islands 'due to lowered thermal buffering.' Both SUPPORTED.

Both affirm the empirical temperature monitoring evidence (C96-C97). OpenEval notes this provides direct mechanistic support despite being collected in only one year (2022) on 20 islands, while peer reviewers acknowledge it as important support for thermal buffering hypothesis. Both SUPPORTED.

Both address the mixed patterns in area effects (C69-C70). OpenEval notes complexity for cold-adapted species suggesting multiple mechanisms, while peer reviewers acknowledge 'Island area, in contrast, had a more mixed role in moderating colonization/extinction rates across species.' Both SUPPORTED with appropriate acknowledgment of complexity.

Both support the mechanistic interpretations (C8, C95). OpenEval notes appropriate caution in identifying dispersal limitation and microclimate buffering as 'primary proxies,' while peer reviewers affirm authors 'present interesting mechanisms without being too bold on their findings.' Both SUPPORTED.

Both address dispersal limitation mechanisms (C95). OpenEval provides detailed species-level evidence (15/15 and 21/23 patterns), while peer reviewers affirm the interpretation of dispersal limitation effects. Both SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on study design and methodology (C3-C4, C110-C120). OpenEval details the methodological documentation and sampling protocols, while peer reviewers praise 'extensive bird monitoring data (9 surveys per year per island) across 36 islands' and describe methodologies as 'appropriate and validated.' Both SUPPORTED.

Both affirm the climate warming context (C40, C121). OpenEval notes the significant warming trend is statistically supported with appropriate metrics, while peer reviewers confirm the study covers a period of 'consistent climatic warming.' Both SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on statistical methodology (C130-C135). OpenEval details the MSOM approach for imperfect detection and Bayesian validation (C132), while peer reviewers affirm 'extensive modeling frameworks' and 'appropriate and validated methodologies.' Both SUPPORTED.

Divergence on island isolation metric (C111). OpenEval finds the methodology well-documented and SUPPORTED, while peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY, noting the metric 'seems a bit too oversimplified' but acknowledge authors found a signal supporting their method. Different evaluation types (SUPPORTED vs UNCERTAIN).

OpenEval evaluates STI methodology and its lack of correlation with ecological traits (C41-C49, C122-C127) as SUPPORTED with appropriate robustness checks. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses the STI metric or its validation.

OpenEval supports the inference about within-region dynamics (C80) and STI as vulnerability indicator (C82-C83) based on strong relationships in the data. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these specific interpretations about STI and vulnerability.

OpenEval affirms the acknowledgment of heterogeneity in species responses (C93-C94) as SUPPORTED, noting this demonstrates appropriate scientific caution. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this nuanced observation about variation.

OpenEval evaluates conservation recommendations (C101-C103) as SUPPORTED but notes they are inferences about management implications rather than direct empirical results. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these specific conservation recommendations.

OpenEval rates a priori hypotheses about mechanisms (C25-C26, C32, C36-C37) as UNCERTAIN, noting they are expectations illustrated in Figure 1 rather than empirical findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation distinguishes these hypotheses from results.

OpenEval rates speculative predictions about future trends (C88-C90) as UNCERTAIN, noting they extend beyond the 10-year study period and lack empirical validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these future predictions.

OpenEval rates post-hoc speculation about predation effects (C100) as UNCERTAIN, noting it is explicitly acknowledged as speculation without direct data. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses this speculative mechanism for unexpected patterns.
